title: Infant respiratory syncytial virus and childhood asthma: a nationwide phenotyping, sibling-controlled, and genome-wide association study

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines whether early-life respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection causes childhood recurrent wheeze or asthma (RW/A), focusing on causality, shared genetic liability, and distinct phenotypic trajectories in Finnish and Nordic populations.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review synthesizes nationwide registry data and Nordic genetic cohorts, including 965,312 Finnish children (1998–2014), 527,776 full siblings, and 15,667 RW/A-discordant sibling pairs, alongside a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of RSV susceptibility (3,107 cases, 92,031 controls) and two-sample Mendelian randomisation (2SMR) using 155 asthma-associated variants.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: RSV-associated RW/A shows higher inhaled medication use at ages 1–2 years but lower use after age 4, with lower mean blood eosinophils (0.34 vs 0.39*10e9/L; p=0.003) compared to RW/A without RSV hospitalisation. RSV hospitalisation is associated with RW/A in discordant sibling pairs (OR 2.8; 95% CI 2.4–3.2), and GWAS identifies an RSV association at APBB1IP (rs787036; beta=0.209; p=8.80*10e-9).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not resolve whether shared genetic or environmental factors fully explain the RSV-asthma association, as unaffected siblings also show elevated RW/A prevalence. analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review prioritises long-term outcomes for RSV prevention trials and monitoring, suggesting that RSV-associated RW/A follows a distinct trajectory that may inform targeted interventions and surveillance strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the causal link between early-life RSV infection and childhood asthma using nationwide Finnish and Nordic cohorts. A GWAS identifies a novel RSV susceptibility locus (APBB1IP), and Mendelian randomisation suggests asthma genetic liability does not drive RSV susceptibility. Key gaps include unresolved mechanisms and the need for replication of genetic findings.
